title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger
author: Akshay Balsubramani
abstract: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's.

title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
author: Benjamin T. Pike
abstract: Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs.

title: Where ADS Crashes Differ: A Harmonized Comparison Against Human Baselines
author: Doyeon Jang
abstract: Crash-rate comparisons between automated driving systems (ADS) and human drivers require an exposure denominator that only a few operators publish. We instead ask a composition question: given a crash, does the mix of crash types differ between ADS and human-driven vehicles? The question needs no mileage and can therefore cover every ADS operator. We assemble the NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO) ADS incident files across both file generations into 2,450 distinct in-scope incidents (2021-2026), of which 828 fall within the 2021-2024 window covered by the Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS), the national police-reported human comparator. A schema-constrained large language model (LLM) codes each SGO narrative into the CRSS crash-type taxonomy. Because SGO compels reporting far below the police-reporting threshold, we bracket reportability with an objective severity floor and a reasonable-person rubric, and claim a difference only where it survives both. Two composition differences hold under every reportability definition, tow definition and weighting of the human side, and under both definitions of driverless operation: turn-across-path crashes are under-represented among ADS crashes (0.23-0.46x the CRSS share under the primary driverless definition) and so are single-vehicle crashes (0.19-0.56x). In severity-floor rear-end crashes the ADS vehicle is the striking party at a quasi-induced-exposure ratio of 0.121 (95% CI [0.05, 0.23]) against a human baseline of 1.000. If the ADS vehicle is also struck more often than its exposure implies, this ratio overstates the ADS-human difference. We also document three pitfalls in the federal data: an operator-specific coding of driverless operation, a tow-away criterion confounded by fleet recovery practice, and an occupancy confound that accounts for about 42% of the apparent ADS-human severity gap.

title: Strategic Tanking in Stable Matching Markets
author: James P. Bailey
abstract: Motivated by a broad literature in psychology, organizational behavior, and matching markets, we introduce strategic tanking: an agent deliberately makes themselves less attractive to selected potential partners in order to improve their eventual assignment. Unlike traditional manipulation in stable matching, a tanker does not misreport whom they prefer; instead, they influence how others rank them. We show that tanking has a striking connection to classical preference manipulation. Cutoff tanking, in which an agent tanks with every potential partner below a chosen threshold, has exactly the same effect on the stable set as truncating one's own preference list at that threshold. Thus an agent can reproduce the power of a classical truncation while leaving their own preferences unchanged and every match acceptable. Arbitrary tanking, however, can go substantially further: under proposer-deferred acceptance, tanking equilibria can lie outside the sincere stable set. More broadly, whenever the sincere stable set contains multiple matchings, profitable strategic behavior remains available through either traditional preference manipulation or tanking, even when one side is restricted to honestly reporting their own preferences.

title: A General Theoretical Framework for Transformed Geometric Pattern Matching in Music
author: David Meredith
abstract: In this paper, we present a framework of concepts, terminology and notation for geometric pattern matching, centred around the idea of a {\em transformation class}. After formally defining the concept of a transformation class, we provide detailed definitions of a number of specific transformation classes that are particularly relevant to pattern matching and pattern discovery in music, which is the primary application domain within which the framework has been developed. We then provide formal definitions of the notions of {\em match}, {\em occurrence}, {\em maximal match\/} and {\em maximal occurrence\/} and prove some results relating to these concepts. We then define and explore in detail the idea of an {\em occurrence set\/} and the more general notion of a {\em heterogeneous occurrence set}. Finally, we explore in detail the concept of {\em transformational equivalence}, including a consideration of {\em transformation groups}, along with the group-theoretic and transformational equivalence properties of selected transformation classes.

title: Treedepth is NP-Hard on Planar Graphs of Maximum Degree 3
author: Kolja Kühn
abstract: Treedepth is an important parameter in algorithmic graph theory. It is known that the problem of computing the treedepth of a graph is NP-hard. It has been an open problem whether treedepth can be computed in polynomial time when the input graph is restricted to be planar, or of bounded degree. Assuming $P \neq NP$, we answer both questions in the negative: Under polynomial-time Turing reductions, it is NP-hard to compute the treedepth of planar graphs with maximum degree 3. This degree bound is best possible, since treedepth can be computed efficiently on graphs of maximum degree 2.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
author: Ronak Bhalgami
abstract: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $γ$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

title: Capacity Meets the Four Subspace Problem: Distributed Linear Computation and the Cross-Ratio
author: Hua Sun
abstract: $K$ users each observe a fixed linear function of common data over a finite field of characteristic $p$, and a server must recover another fixed linear function with zero error from one message sent by each user. The capacity, the minimum total number of symbols the users send per computed instance, depends only on the configuration of subspaces formed by these linear functions. We study the instance in which three users observe $\boldsymbol{a}$, $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}+\boldsymbol{b}$ and the server wants $\boldsymbol{a}+λ\boldsymbol{b}$. The four functions span four lines in a plane with cross-ratio $λ$, the smallest instance of the four subspace problem of representation theory. It is the smallest configuration whose capacity is not determined by the dimensions of the subspaces formed by sums and intersections: these dimensions are the same for every $λ$, but the capacity depends on the cross-ratio and on the prime subfield. For the harmonic cross-ratios, $λ=-1$, $λ=2$ or $2λ=1$, it is $2$: every zero-error code reveals $(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b})$ to the server, so no code beats having two users send their observations. For $λ$ outside the prime subfield it is the cut-set bound $3/2$, achieved by codes linear over the prime subfield, while codes linear over the field need $2$. For the other $λ$ in the prime subfield it lies in $[3p/(2p-1),2]$, so no code at any block length approaches the cut-set bound. The qualitative separation persists under vanishing error for uniform data: the cut-set bound is tight exactly for $λ$ outside the prime subfield. The four-line instance is also exact repair of one node of a $[4,2]$ MDS storage code, and the results translate to that setting.

title: The C-3PO Framework: Algorithms for $\#\mathrm{BIS}$-Hard Problems on Graphs with Low Threshold Rank or High Girth
author: Ijay Narang
abstract: We give approximate counting and sampling algorithms for spin models on graphs of low threshold rank or high girth. Given any $n$-vertex graph $G$, let $k_η= k_η(G)$ count normalized-Laplacian eigenvalues strictly below $η$. For $\varepsilon > 0$, an $\varepsilon$-approximate counting algorithm outputs an estimate $\widehat Z$ of the partition function $Z$ satisfying $(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z$ with probability at least $3/4$. An $\varepsilon$-approximate sampling algorithm outputs a configuration whose distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the target distribution. We give the following results: (a) Ferromagnetic Potts. Fix $q\ge2$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $β_0(q,η)$ such that, for every inverse temperature $β\geβ_0$, the zero-field $q$-state Potts model admits approximate counting and sampling algorithms: (i) On arbitrary graphs in time $\exp(O(k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) Fix $Δ\ge 3$. On $Δ$-regular graphs of girth $g$ in time $\exp(O(n e^{-g})) \operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (b) Bipartite hard-core. Fix $Δ\ge3$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $λ_0(Δ,η)$ such that, for every fugacity $λ\geλ_0$, the hard-core model admits approximate counting and sampling: (i) On $Δ$-regular vertex-transitive bipartite graphs in time $\exp(O (k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) On $Δ$-regular bipartite graphs of girth $g$ in $\exp(O(n e^{- g}))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ All four results follow from verifying the hypotheses of a new framework we call C-3PO. At a high level, the C-3PO algorithm proceeds by enumerating small cuts and reconstructing the original measure through cluster expansions. Underlying the algorithm is an improvement of subspace enumeration methods via active regression.

title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
author: Hanyu Yang
abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.

title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
author: Eduardo C. Garrido-Merchán
abstract: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

title: Optimal Average Distortion for Non-Expansive Embeddings of Euclidean Metrics into the Line: With applications to cut-matching games and vertex expansion
author: Jack Spalding-Jamieson
abstract: We show that any $n$-point Euclidean metric admits a non-expansive embedding into the line with average distortion at most $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}}\right)$, matching a known lower bound. We also present two applications of this result. First, we give a cut-player strategy with an optimal spectral guarantee for the undirected cut-matching game. Second, we give an improved spectral approximation for vertex expansion in high-degree graphs.

title: Type classifiers
author: Martin E. Bidlingmaier
abstract: We extend dependent type theory by type classifiers and construct an interpretation in the category of contextual categories with families. Type classifiers extend contexts by type variables, complementing the usual context extensions by term variables of specified types. This allows statements with arbitrary type parameters to be formulated without assuming a universe. We show that substituting isomorphic types induces isomorphisms between the resulting types even in extensional type theory, giving an analogue of the invariance supplied by the univalence axiom in homotopy type theory. Omitting function types from the theory, so that all type formers are covariant, extends this naturality to arbitrary, possibly noninvertible maps.

title: Completeness and Cost of Retrieval Structures for Multi-Tool Requests in LLM Agents
author: Shuyang Zhang
abstract: An agent that must call several tools to fulfill a request fails when the tool retriever omits any one of them, yet tool retrievers are mostly built and evaluated on queries requiring a single tool. We compare representatives of six retrieval structures (flat lexical and dense retrieval, LLM query decomposition, LLM-navigated hierarchies, server-then-tool matching, dependency graphs, and trained set-level retrievers) across two multi-tool testbeds: 345 AppWorld queries with expert dependency labels and 103 MCP-Bench tasks over 257 MCP tools. We measure completeness@k, the share of queries whose entire required tool set appears in the top k, alongside the LLM calls, tokens, and latency that each structure incurs at retrieval time. A motivating analysis on all 7,961 ToolRet queries shows that aggregate completeness mixes two regimes: completeness at 10 is .58 to .67 on single-target queries and .08 to .17 on queries with four or more targets, and the ordering of retrievers on single-target queries reverses on multi-target ones. Across the two testbeds, none of the compared structures that is untrained on the testbed and makes at most one LLM call per query completes more than 10% of AppWorld queries at k = 16. The two structures that do better incur different costs: a set-level retriever trained on 75 to 90 in-domain queries reaches .33 on AppWorld and .58 on MCP-Bench with no LLM calls, while an LLM-navigated hierarchy reaches .30 and .40 with a median of 31 to 38 LLM calls and about five minutes per query. Their failure modes also differ: the trained retriever mostly ranks the missing tools just below the cutoff, whereas the hierarchy finds the target API and stops before collecting its prerequisites. In a downstream check with the official AppWorld agent, tasks with a complete retrieved set succeeded 21 of 21 times, whereas incomplete ones succeeded 2 of 39 times.

title: On approximate support versions of Donoho--Stark uncertainty principles for $k$-Hadamard operators
author: Rami Ayoush
abstract: In this paper we present results related to Donoho--Stark type uncertainty principles that were proved in the article "The uncertainty principle: variations on a theme" by Wigderson and Wigderson for $k$-Hadamard operators in the finite-dimensional setting. Namely, the authors showed that Donoho-Stark principles can be generalized to versions for approximate supports with respect to norms $\ell^{p}$ for $p=1$ and $p=2$. In the second case they assumed the so-called speciality condition, namely that a suitable matrix satisfies $A^{*}A = kI$. First we show that such theorems cannot be generalized to $p>1$ if matrices are not special $k$-Hadamard. Next we prove Donoho-Stark type principle for special $k$-Hadamard operators for $\ell^{p}$ norms within the range $1\leq p\leq 2$. Finally, we show that such theorems are false for $p>2$ even in the presence of the speciality condition.

title: SketchMate: Agentic Geometric Reasoning for Zero-Shot Precision Insertion
author: Jiaming Wang
abstract: Inserting an unseen part requires sub-millimetre precision and the correct orientation of keyed features. Current zero-shot agentic manipulation methods built on vision-language models (VLMs) produce spatial outputs that are far too coarse for this. We propose to let a VLM build a sketch model of the task, i.e., a few geometric primitives and two mate frames, which a VLM agent measures with geometric tools in multi-view depth and which a standard planner and compliant controller execute. Because a sketch describes the parts independently of their placement, the robot needs to build it only once per task. A sketch memory stores each agent run and transfers the stored sketch to later placements by point-cloud registration, so that the VLM is called only for unfamiliar parts. After grasping the part, the robot inspects both mating faces at close range and corrects the sketch by shape matching. On 69 simulated insertion episodes, our method inserts 88% of the parts at the assembled pose in a strict kinematic test, while ReKep and MOKA with the same VLM insert none. On new placements of eight tasks, reusing one stored run inserts as many parts as calling the agent in each episode, and it produces the sketch in 3.4 s instead of about 90 s.

title: Exploring Bad Minima in Transfer Learning
author: Mina Remeli
abstract: Transfer learning is a highly successful learning paradigm in deep learning which leverages knowledge from one task and applies it to another. Despite its success, the necessary conditions for knowledge transfer are unclear and require further research. In this dissertation, our aim is to understand transferability a little better by answering the following question: Does good generalization on a source task necessarily imply transferability to a related target task? We hypothesize the answer is negative, and attempt to find counterexamples via adversarial attacks on the transfer learning procedure. Over three types of adversarial attacks, our empirical results show a strong relationship between generalization on the source task and transferability. These results do not rule out generalization on the source task as a sufficient condition for successful transfer.

title: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity
author: Alexander Safonov
abstract: Morphogenesis of diatom silica shells involves a sequence of topological transitions: initially separate ribs grow and branch, then merge through bridges, leaving a regular network of pores. Existing models based on diffusion-limited aggregation or reaction-diffusion reproduce either branching or pore formation, but not both within a single framework. Here we propose a two-stage model of diffusion-driven morphogenesis with evolving connectivity. The model is formulated on a fixed finite element mesh with a density field on an active layer. Stage 1 reproduces dendritic growth, where a stimulus based on the local diffusive flux exceeds a threshold. Stage 2 uses an inverted stimulus, where high local flux suppresses precipitation, stabilizing pores between the dendrites. The update rules are analogous to sensitivity in density-based topology optimization and to strain energy density in bone remodeling. The model predicts distinct morphological regimes on each stage, controlled by the respective thresholds. For a reference calculation, the predicted pore network is regular, with approximately uniform spacing, and pores are absent near the domain edges, consistent with observations on diatom valves. The model provides a unified framework for describing both stages of silica morphogenesis and suggests a route for comparing computational predictions with cryo-electron tomography data.

title: Higher-Order Kinematic Derivatives for Aspect-Preserving Real-Time Numerical Inverse Kinematics
author: Steffan Lloyd
abstract: This paper leverages the higher-order kinematic derivatives of serial robots to achieve efficient, aspect-preserving real-time inverse kinematics. First, a family of higher-order solvers is derived, with a necessary orientation-error correction map, yielding the QuIK4 and QuIK5 methods with fourth- and fifth-order convergence. Second, an aspect-preserving step limiter extrapolates the Jacobian determinant along the step to predict and avoid singularities, shortening steps only when they head toward a singularity rather than when the current iterate is ill-conditioned. Third, a Hermite-interpolation certifier verifies the aspect of each answer, and a certified restart algorithm recovers failures from proven same-aspect seeds. The proposed methods are shown to outperform prior methods, reducing failures by up to four orders of magnitude and nearly eliminating aspect switching at tracking-level errors. A C++ library is released with ROS 2 integration.

title: When Architectural Spaces Start to Act
author: Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen
abstract: Architectural spaces are increasingly gaining robotic capabilities. Architectural robots such as robotic partitions, ceilings, furniture, facades, and other spatial components can autonomously move and reconfigure in response to occupants' needs and activities. Yet, when architectural robots start shaping the spatial conditions in which people continuously live, work, and interact, we may begin to experience the architectural space itself as robotic. What does this shift mean for how we inhabit such spaces? Drawing on our previous studies, I reflect on how architectural robots interact with people not only through their motions, but also through the spatial configurations that persist after those motions stop; how their actions may benefit some occupants while disadvantaging others; and how multiple robots may together make a whole architectural space appear to act. I argue that as computation gains the capacity to physically reconfigure our environments, interaction extends beyond the moment of computational action into the spatial conditions that people continue to inhabit. Understanding robotic architecture therefore requires us to look beyond short-term human-robot interaction and toward how people inhabit, negotiate, and maintain control over spaces that can autonomously reconfigure.

title: A Fully Polynomial Randomized Approximation Scheme for Hypergraph Unreliability
author: Zhijie Zheng
abstract: We give a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for all-terminal unreliability in explicitly represented undirected hypergraphs of arbitrary rank. The algorithm estimates the probability that independent hyperedge failures disconnect the hypergraph, allowing a different rational failure probability for every edge. For a common failure probability, this improves the quasi-polynomial approximation schemes of Cen, Li, and Panigrahi to polynomial time and answers the polynomial-time approximation question reiterated in their subsequent work on graphs. The construction turns their representative-survival bound into an importance sampler whose relative second moment is bounded solely in terms of the number of vertices. We protect one randomly chosen representative pair during contraction, correct the path likelihood, and divide by the number of pairs surviving at the end. The resulting unbiased estimator has relative second moment at most $\binom n2$, even when unreliability is exponentially small. A minimum-cut normalization makes this estimator implementable with polynomially bounded precision: the residual likelihood becomes a survival probability in an auxiliary absorbing process, which admits rational discretization with a fixed random-bit budget. Logarithmic rate rounding and an exact weighted minimum cut extend the construction to unequal rational failure probabilities. The algorithm's worst-case running time and random-bit usage are polynomial in the input length, the inverse relative error, and $\log(1/δ)$ for confidence $1-δ$.

title: From fleet trajectories to single-cell promises: hierarchically weighted conformal prediction for battery SOH monitoring
author: Xiangyu Liu
abstract: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.

title: A Preconditioned Quantum Linear Solver for Periodic Two-Phase Heat Conduction with Mesh-Independent Condition Number
author: Krishnan Suresh
abstract: We consider here computational homogenization of a periodic two-phase conduction problem. Quantum linear-system algorithms for its finite element discretization are limited by the condition number of the stiffness matrix. This condition number grows quadratically with the number of elements per side. Classically, preconditioning by the homogeneous (single-phase) operator bounds the condition number by the conductivity contrast, for every mesh size. On a quantum computer, however, a preconditioner encoded as a separate factor multiplies the subnormalizations, and the quadratic dependency returns. In this paper, we absorb the closed-form inverse square root of the homogeneous operator into the finite element factors. The preconditioned operator then becomes the product of a norm-preserving gradient operator $\mat{V}$, a diagonal matrix of scaled conductivities, and $\mat{V}^T$. Each factor has norm at most one. The block encoding therefore has subnormalization one, and its condition number is bounded by just the conductivity contrast, for every mesh size and in every dimension. The operator $\mat{V}$ is applied as a quantum Fourier transform, a small rotation at each wavenumber, and an inverse transform. Quantum singular value transformation then block-encodes the inverse of the preconditioned operator. We test the method numerically on three periodic cells with up to $10^6$ unknowns. The results confirm that the condition number does not depend on the mesh, and the energy-norm error of the inverse is below the polynomial tolerance at every mesh. On meshes of $4 \times 4$ and $8 \times 8$ elements, we also build the entire inverse as one Qiskit circuit and simulate it by state vector, with the rotation at each wavenumber built from uniformly controlled rotations. The output state agrees with the finite element solution to within the polynomial tolerance.

title: OpenVIO: A Versatile Open-Source Visual-Inertial Odometry System
author: Seungwon Choi
abstract: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) is a fundamental topic in robotics research. Beyond research, VIO has been adopted in a wide range of products. In this manuscript, we present OpenVIO, an open-source VIO system for research and practical applications. It is released under the MIT license. OpenVIO supports pinhole and fisheye cameras and extends this support to stitched 360° images. We describe each part of the system together with its design considerations. We also report benchmark results with other open-source VIO systems on public datasets. OpenVIO is available as open source at https://github.com/93won/openvio.

title: Risk-Sensitive Mission Planning for Multi-Target On-Orbit Inspection via Distributional Reinforcement Learning
author: Adam Abdin
abstract: Multi-target on-orbit servicing missions require planning tools that can adapt to evolving operational conditions while accounting for the outcome variability inherent to safety-critical spaceflight. This paper presents an adaptive planning approach for multi-target servicing campaigns in low Earth orbit and applies it to inspection missions flown by a low-thrust servicer. The approach is based on Distributional Reinforcement Learning, which learns the full distribution of mission returns and thereby supports explicit risk-sensitive decision-making at each planning step. Specifically, a Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN) agent selects which target to inspect next by jointly considering the expectation and the variance of the predicted return through a mean-variance criterion. The mission environment models circular orbits with a spread in inclination and uses Edelbaum's combined-manoeuvre low-thrust transfer estimates. The observation comprises the orbital elements, the visit history, the observed risk state of each target and the remaining mission-time budget. The risk state of each target changes stochastically during the campaign, making the outcome of an inspection uncertain and creating operationally meaningful distinctions between risk-neutral and risk-averse planning strategies. Because the mission-time budget generally admits only a subset of the candidate targets, the planner must also select which targets to inspect. Numerical experiments on scenarios with five target satellites show that one risk-aversion weight moves the policy across a range of mean return and return variance, over an unchanged environment and reward. Risk-averse agents reduce the variance of the episodic return by approximately one half relative to risk-neutral agents and lower the probability of a mission loss, at a cost in mean return. To validate the learned policies, the efficient frontier, which gives the highest mean return attainable at each level of return variance, is computed exactly by enumerating the admissible visit orders. At equal variance, the learned policies lie close to this frontier in mean return, and the risk-averse policies have a lower probability of a mission loss than the frontier policies.

title: A Constructive Orbit-Based Theory of Learnability
author: Yunied Puig
abstract: We develop a finite-dimensional orbit framework for constructing data-adapted dictionaries, sparse realizations, and predictive extensions. The method uses wrapped weighted shifts to generate orbit dictionaries and local interpolation maps from independent orbit representatives, turning the learning problem into three explicit tasks: scaffold discovery, sparse realization on the discovered dictionary, and prediction through learned sparse coordinates. We introduce CCDS as the main constructive ingredient: a deviation-controlled sparse realization procedure that recovers MP/OMP-type behavior at the minimal-deviation boundary while allowing feasible interior paths with prescribed residual geometry that is inaccessible to MP/OMP. We prove generic orbit independence, exact block interpolation with norm control, observable bounds on sparse approximation distortion, sparse realization guarantees on selected supports, and fixed-path stability under admissible perturbations of the block interpolants. These results connect sparse approximation, interpolation, and finite-dimensional operator dynamics through the construction and analysis of data-induced orbit dictionaries. Experiments on synthetic geometry, controlled realization tests, and standard classification benchmarks show that selected orbit scaffolds have substantially better matched-rank projection behavior than random orbit or unstructured alternatives, that CCDS attains near-zero realization error at the minimal-deviation boundary, and that predictors trained from the sparse CCDS certificates give competitive performance.

title: Lowered crossover points of Anthropic's subexponential 3-SAT algorithm
author: Ruhollah Majdoddin
abstract: The October 2026 refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis count satisfying assignments in time $2^{o(n)}$, but an asymptotic bound does not say from which input size, the crossover point, they beat the best known algorithms. We make the #3-SAT recursion of Anthropic's algorithm explicit and lower its crossover points, computed from the main term of the proved bound, by proved changes. For the bound in the number $m$ of clauses, at clause density one, the crossover point drops to about $2^{420}$ clauses from $2^{33858}$; for general 3-SAT, in the number $n$ of variables, our estimate drops to $2^{8.6\cdot10^9}$ variables from $2^{2.2\cdot10^{12}}$. With integer tables the recursion counts, for every $j$, the assignments satisfying exactly $j$ clauses in time $2^{O(m/\sqrt{\log m})}$. We observe that this refutes the Sparse Max-3-SAT Hypothesis of Alman and Vassilevska Williams, which also follows from either refutation by the reduction of Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane, and we lower the crossover point of this computation to about $2^{1016}$ clauses from $2^{68364}$. The distance is structural: we define a rewrite-and-merge class that contains the recursion and all our constructions, and prove that in the main-term model no grid algorithm in it can gain for general 3-SAT below about $2^{6000}$ variables. For two balanced homogeneous merges we prove with quantum functionals an exponent of at least $(\log_2K)^{-3}$ per edge bit, which excludes running times $2^{n^{1-c}}$. Independently of SAT, we formalise the algorithm as a model of computation, Signed Network Sums, which contains rank-one methods and contraction trees. On the complete graph with four nodes, one-level constructions contract the network in $N^{23/6}$ if $ω=2$ and in about $N^{3.93}$ on the current (preprint) matrix-multiplication curve, below the bound $N^4$ of every rank-one method or contraction tree.

title: List 3-Coloring in tame classes of graphs in quasipolynomial time
author: Paweł Rzążewski
abstract: A class of graphs $\mathcal{G}$ is tame if there is a constant c such that every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{G}$ has at most $n^c$ minimal separators. Many important graph classes are tame, including chordal graphs, permutation graphs, and circle graphs. Several fundamental problems, most notably Max Weight Independent Set, can be solved in polynomial time on every tame class, which explains in a unified way their tractability on all these classes. We show that List 3-Coloring can be solved in quasipolynomial time on every tame class of graphs.

title: Serial Rug-Pull-Like Exits on Pump.fun: Team-Level Evidence and Its Sensitivity to Team Construction
author: Fail Gafarov
abstract: We study repeated, team-associated selling around sharp collapses of Pump.fun tokens in several deliberately selected data windows, separating the measurement from claims of fraud, common ownership or realized profit. Because token prices derived from trade amounts are not fully reliable, we compare a price-based screen with a screen that uses only the bonding-curve reserve and SOL amounts; most price-based episodes are also found by the reserve screen. Episodes concentrate in groups well beyond a within-hour label-shuffle benchmark, and most of them are collapses sold by a single creator wallet. The recorded own-token cash flow of the identified groups is positive in most windows and negative in a few, but the sign of the negative results is fragile: it changes with the screen, with the definition of a group, with the length of the window and with trading costs of about two per cent per side. A daily SOL price covariate shows no association with the incidence of episodes. An agent-based simulation of a team exit on a bonding curve, extended with a latent attention to each token and calibrated to marginal moments of the data, shows that the team's result depends mainly on the attention that tokens attract, on fees and on the team's own trading, that continual trading by the team is costly and that reacting to the inflow of other traders adds little. The model reproduces the sign of group-level results but not the early exits that are common in the data. Missing token transfers, verified migration labels and human-labelled validation prevent identifying operator profit or fraud prevalence.

title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
author: Michael Farrell
abstract: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

title: On $t$-designs supported by self-orthogonal codes
author: Masaaki Harada
abstract: We study self-orthogonal $t$-$(v,k,λ)$ designs satisfying the condition that the codes generated by the designs are self-orthogonal codes whose codewords of minimum weight $k$ correspond to the blocks. A classification of such designs is given under the conditions that $t\geq \lfloor k/4\rfloor+1\geq2$ and $t \le 11$. This yields a classification of self-orthogonal codes of minimum weight $k$ whose codewords of minimum weight form a $t$-design under the same conditions.

title: New bounds for online coloring three-colorable graphs
author: Yaqiao Li
abstract: We prove new lower and upper bounds for online coloring of three-colorable graphs, improving classical bounds of Vishwanathan [FOCS'1990] that have stood for more than three decades. For the lower bound against deterministic algorithms, we improve Vishwanathan's $Ω(\log^2n)$ to \(\exp\!\bigl(Ω((\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})\bigr)\). For the upper bound of randomized algorithms, we give a randomized algorithm that achieves $O(\sqrt{n})$ improving Vishwanathan's $O(\sqrt{n \log n})$. Technically, for the lower bound construction, we introduce the language of $t$-fold coloring for simpler description of recursive construction, and the notion of post-degree for future control, and use the flexibility of two-sided colors of bipartite graph, constructed using the independent set amplification method of Vishwanathan, as building blocks to ensure three-colorability. The randomized algorithm integrates, in a new way, some of the ideas in offline coloring of Wigderson and Blum with ideas of Vishwanathan in the online setting, such as the degree control from Wigderson, the offline-monochromatic class from Blum, and the anchor-sampling from Vishwanathan and the CBIP algorithm by Lov{á}sz, Saks and Trotter.

title: Improved Approximation Guarantees for Periodic-Review Stochastic Inventory Control
author: Danny Segev
abstract: In periodic-review stochastic inventory control, replenishment policies must balance holding and backlogging costs while responding to uncertain demands and evolving forecasts that may be arbitrarily correlated and nonstationary. In this general information setting, Levi, P{á}l, Roundy, and Shmoys (Mathematics of Operations Research 2007) established that the fully adaptive optimum can be approximated within factor $2$, which had remained the best-known performance guarantee since then. Their marginal cost accounting and dual-balancing framework made this comparison possible without computing optimal decisions across future trajectories, opening a broad research program on approximation algorithms for stochastic inventory systems. We break this long-standing barrier for periodic-review stochastic inventory control, showing how to compete against the fully adaptive benchmark within factor $\frac{ e }{ e-1 } \approx 1.582$ while retaining general demand correlations and evolving forecasts. We attain these advances by discovering a structural connection between marginal inventory accounting and weighted stopping problems, where each unit's conditional holding charge forms a supermartingale, while postponing its order incurs a history-dependent backlog charge. To leverage the random thresholding approach of Ma and Tzamos (ICML 2023) in this context, we develop a potential-function analysis, leading to an $\frac{ e }{ e-1 }$-approximation with respect to any unit's stopping problem. Subsequently, our common-threshold policy coordinates these marginal decisions into a global replenishment policy without additional loss.

title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $ε$-close Surrogates
author: Ziye Ma
abstract: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $ε$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(ε)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. Assuming each matrix entry is observed independently, we establish quantitative recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence, and discuss how such assumptions can further strengthen our results.

title: Certifying Retraining Regret through Residual Structure
author: Peida Li
abstract: We certify a fixed ridge predictor's regret against full-feature retraining over every continuous completion of an interval-valued table. Our main theorem gives verifiable original-row residual conditions for a uniform error bound independent of nuisance-feature scale and rank, with an asymptotically sharp leading constant and quantitative leakage stability. Full-rank constructions separate certification dimension from feature dimension, including examples requiring directions beyond the candidate. Observed-row anchors make the conditions computable, while exact row geometry and global search return valid upper bounds and feasible original-table witnesses. A finite-scale contraction and common-domain moment fallback implement the structural result. Four real-world tasks retain all model features and certify twenty rank-three instances to width $10^{-5}$. Their primary median widths improve over centered moments. Joint residual refinement additionally certifies all twenty new response-independent masks to the same precision within 76.21 seconds. For a concrete fixed-point predictor contract, pure energy certifies thirteen of fifteen stopping decisions in ten seconds, versus five for moments. Refinement certifies all fifteen within 91.68 seconds at the same objective threshold.

title: When History Overrides Intent: Relational Schema Lock-In in Human-LLM Interaction
author: Wei Yang
abstract: Long-context interaction and persistent memory allow LLM assistants to develop history-grounded understandings of users. When users change direction, however, an understanding built through earlier exchanges may conflict with their current instruction. We introduce relational schema lock-in to describe cases in which an assistant grants that accumulated understanding authority to override the current instruction without user authorization for the intervention. Study 1 documents reports of AI assistants using prior interactions to question or alter requested actions. Study 2 reproduces the pattern across controlled histories and six models: models retained history-grounded positions but differed in whether and how those positions shaped task execution. In Study 3 with 360 participants, artifact substitution preserved task completion while reducing faithful enactment: 75.0% sent the AI's suspension letter, including 11 participants who reported cancellation as their final stated intent. Overt resistance reduced task completion while leaving sent artifacts faithful.

title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation
author: Pengfei Zheng
abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.

title: rl_rob: A transparent, from-scratch Python library for teaching reinforcement learning from tabular methods to deep policy gradients
author: Abdulrahman Altahhan
abstract: rl_rob is an open-source Python library for teaching reinforcement learning. It implements the arc of a modern course, from tabular temporal-difference learning through linear function approximation to deep value-based and policy-gradient methods, with every algorithm written from first principles so that its update rule is visible in a few lines of code. All agents share one interface, so learners can compare methods directly across stages and trace a deep reinforcement learning update from the temporal-difference error to the weight change. The library supports teaching and assessment in which students implement, modify and explain update rules, rather than only produce working code.

title: Truthful and Admissible Principal--Agent Testing with Nuisance Parameters
author: Aaditya Ramdas
abstract: Statistical contracts reward experimenters according to the evidence produced by a costly study, so the reward rule influences both who participates and what they report. Principal--agent testing theory explains how to prevent ineffective proposals from being profitable. We ask when such contracts can also elicit honest parameter reports if the decision concerns a mean effect but the variance or distributional shape is unknown. Under risk neutrality and a fixed participation cost, we construct menus of e-values --- nonnegative normalized rewards with expected value at most one under every null --- such that (i) agents who know they are null have no incentive to participate, (ii) every alternative type earns positive expected profit and is thus incentivized to participate, (iii) truthful reporting uniquely maximizes expected their reward, (iv) and each contract is admissible: its payouts cannot be pointwise improved while retaining null validity. For Gaussian observations, we treat separately agents who know both mean and variance and agents who know only their mean; in the latter case, truthfulness holds at every variance without requiring a nuisance prior. Multi-sample extensions preserve these incentives and can reward accumulating evidence. Beyond Gaussian models, we show that two independent nonnegative observations suffice to elicit any finite mean above a positive null threshold, without any further distributional knowledge, but one observation cannot combine strict mean elicitation with individual admissibility on this class. Finally, we distinguish the existence of useful tests from the identification needed for truthful contracts. Boundedness is not required, and finitely many null constraints do not by themselves guarantee admissible elicitation.

title: Architectural Debt Enforcement under Incomplete Observation: A Controlled Study of Ratchets and Evidence Qualification
author: Zhiheng Zhang
abstract: Architectural debt gates must distinguish an allowed change from an incompletely observed one. We study a decision contract separating observation qualification, prohibited relation identity, inherited debt and authorized baseline updates. Across 240 fixed files from four repositories, the current observer and programmatic reference jointly qualify 166 files (69.17%), all with exact reference-relative edge agreement; 74 remain reference-UNKNOWN. Coverage varies from 13/60 to 59/60 by repository. On 480 constructed state scenarios sharing 60 source anchors, both the candidate ratchet and mature dependency-cruiser baseline match every expected outcome, whereas static and count-only baselines match 420 and 360. These results do not establish candidate superiority. Preserved failures include nine additional false-PASS probes and 120 unqualified full-tree timing attempts. A subsequent generic binding layer rejects 54 specified mismatches, accepts 54 current controls and permits legal repetition. Two bounded package scopes support 40 scenarios and 48 fresh-process functional checks; their costs remain tied to the measured implementations. Diagnostics explain residual uncertainty through type/runtime relations, installation context and generated-artifact provenance. TypeScript 5.9.3 and 6.0.2 yield identical outputs on ten paired emission witnesses, but neither that agreement nor verified release provenance changes the frozen UNKNOWN labels. The contribution is a controlled account of evidence-qualified enforcement and its limits, not language completeness, natural maintenance effectiveness or a new shrinking-baseline algorithm.

title: Generative SDEs with Trainable Diffusion and Density-Based Losses
author: Angxiu Ni
abstract: We develop a divergence-kernel method for jointly optimizing neural SDE drift and diffusion fields and the initial Gaussian distribution, using losses that depend directly on the terminal density. In two- and eight-dimensional Gaussian-mixture experiments, we learn time-independent fields and obtain far fewer off-mode samples than score-based generators with similar parameter counts. The drift attracts samples toward the modes, while the diffusion helps disperse excess probability between them.

title: Random-Sign IBLTs: Calibration-Free Self-Sizing After Decoding Failure
author: Min Wu
abstract: We propose the random-sign Invertible Bloom Lookup Table (IBLT) for calibration-free self-sizing after decoding failure. In a two-round set reconciliation protocol, the receiver uses the failed first-round table to estimate an upper bound on the unknown difference size $d$ and size the second-round table. In standard IBLTs, failure selection couples the overlap bias with the sign composition of the set difference, making practical sizing depend on offline simulation calibration. A shared pseudorandom sign independent of the position mapping removes this dependence while preserving cell fields, field widths, and ideal peeling recovery. We prove exact unbiasedness on every fixed mapping, a Gaussian limit after failure for $d\gg\sqrt M$, and a discrete limit dominated by duplicate edge pairs at smaller scales, where $M$ is the number of cells. These results yield a Skellam upper-bound rule whose conditional miss rate is asymptotically at most the target risk, uniformly over all $d\ge2$, without offline calibration. More than 500 million paired decoding trials and end-to-end protocol experiments support the design. For small differences, the Gaussian rule's conditional miss rate exceeds the target by more than a factor of 8. The Skellam rule meets the target within sampling error across all 189 tested load configurations. Total two-round communication approaches that of an oracle using the true $d$ in the same protocol. With fixed deployment parameters, precomputed table lookup reduces sizing to less than one microsecond, with total protocol time within 0.5 percent of the Gaussian rule.

title: Resource Locks and Fast Unlock for Shared Balances in Certificate-Based Payment Systems
author: Lingkang Shangguan
abstract: Certificate-based payment systems such as FastPay settle a payment with one round of signatures from a quorum of validators and avoid global ordering. The client collects the signatures, and validators never talk to each other. We observe that this client-driven design is complete only as long as no lock is ever undone. Each account has a single writer, a conflict can only come from that writer's own misbehavior, and the account stays locked as the penalty. Stablecoin payments routinely need balances that several accounts debit: treasuries, merchant pools, allowances and subscriptions. There, honest accounts race, locks must be undone, and a quorum certificate held privately by a client can be silently overridden. We prove that no unlock rule is safe in this setting unless certificate formation is visible to validators. We present a hybrid protocol. Personal accounts keep the client-driven FastPay path unchanged. A shared resource is a balance with its own version number and a set of authorized accounts. Transactions on shared resources are submitted to any validator and certified by a two-phase broadcast, ECHO then READY. The admission check requires both the sender's nonce and the resource's nonce to be free. Without contention, this path needs no consensus. When concurrent debits split the votes in any proportion, validators detect the split themselves, freeze the affected resource version, and resolve it with one agreement instance scoped to that version. Losing transactions return their sender nonce. We prove consistency, no overdraft, validity, finality and liveness. The protocol composes with the PDCC reconfiguration protocol.

title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation
author: Yuchen Zhang
abstract: LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 dataset, four heterogeneous detectors emit labels and confidences that we corrupt under a threat model varying the number of corrupted tools, the persistence of the corruption, and the confidence attached to wrong outputs. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.

title: An Empirical Study on Learning Rooftop Solar Potential from Satellite Imagery Directly Without Explicit Geometry
author: Joshua Lee
abstract: Rooftop solar potential estimation often relies on LiDAR, digital surface models (DSMs), or pipelines that explicitly reconstruct roof geometry before estimating solar potential. We propose Direct Rooftop Solar Prediction (DRSP), an end-to-end formulation that maps satellite imagery and coarse regional sunlight information directly to application-level solar outputs. DRSP neither requires explicit geometric representations as input nor predicts roof orientation, slope, height, DSMs, or other geometric quantities as intermediate outputs, and therefore requires no geometric intermediate supervision. To enable large-scale study of this formulation, we develop a programmatic data-curation pipeline that converts per-panel information from the Google Solar API into usable-rooftop masks and spatial solar-energy targets, yielding two geographically distinct datasets containing approximately 60K rooftops from the U.S. Midwest and 87K from Texas. We demonstrate the feasibility of DRSP and systematically characterize the effects of geographic training distribution, model depth, image resolution, regional sunlight conditioning, and heatmap regression objectives. Overall, our results suggest that useful rooftop-scale solar information can be learned directly from 2D imagery without explicit geometric intermediate representations, offering a simpler path toward large-scale solar assessment. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/joshualee124/direct_rooftop_solar_prediction.

title: Memory and Recall of Color Images Using Neural Networks-1 - The Cue-Ball Model based on the Associative Memory Mechanism -
author: Hiroshi Inazawa
abstract: This paper presents a neural network model for storing and recalling color images of different sizes using the Cue BallRecall Net systems [1,2,3,4,5]. The Cue Ball system consists of a Recall Net composed of multiple memory neurons each responsible for memorizing a single, distinct memory and a large number of neurons that represent image patterns. The images used in this study [6] consist of ten images(see Appendix). The pixel values of these images were converted into digital values and used for subsequent processing. Accordingly, the Cue Ball contains ten Cue neurons, corresponding to the ten images stored in memory. The number of pixels varies among the images, and therefore, the number of Recall neurons comprising the Recall Net also varies accordingly. In this study, the number of Recall neurons was prepared between 106,134 and 360,000, depending on the number of pixels in each image. In this simulation, after the connection weights (wjip, vijp) had been learned, we have used the learning and recall algorithms to investigate whether the Cue neuron which had memorized a specific image could be identified by the Recall Net when that a memorized image has been presented. Therefore, the most important simulation result is which Cue neuron responds when a memorized image is presented to the Recall Net. If the Cue neuron that memorizes the presented image responds, its output can be used to obtain the corresponding image data. By adding a BMP header to the resulting image data, the original memorized image can be accurately recalled.

title: Local Budget Benefits, Population Commitment, and Solver Performance: A DGO Case Study with Controlled DE Transfer
author: Shiqi Li
abstract: An evaluated candidate can improve a local search step, alter the population used by later steps, and affect a solver's final result. We distinguish these three questions using Da Gou Gun Optimization (DGO), a population optimizer designed for this study. Its JQ100 configuration evaluates an interpolation candidate during a two-sided probe. We define local budget value, population commitment effects and complete-policy performance, and give an exact example in which a locally better commitment leads to a worse continuation. Short-horizon matched comparisons favor interpolation on eligible quadratic states. Paired continuations yield mixed effect estimates, with primary group intervals spanning zero. Complete-policy comparisons favor JQ100 over the tested classical references in aggregate; a matched-start comparison has favorable means but intervals spanning parity. On 24 boxed BBOB functions, target-truncated geometric-mean error ratios favor JQ100 over the tested classical policies and favor L-SHADE and CMA-ES over JQ100 under the stated initialization and stopping rules. Local evaluation gains, commitment effects and solver competitiveness therefore require separate comparisons.

title: Nonlinear Maps Between Irreducible Representations in Graph Neural Networks
author: Mani Shayestehfar
abstract: Equivariant linear maps cannot mix non-isomorphic irreducible representations, whereas nonlinear activations can. We develop a degree-resolved version of this nonlinear interaction picture and use the resulting block inventory to construct Specht Triple, a residual on unordered graph triples. On a synthetic structural benchmark with a frozen GIN backbone, Specht Triple reduces aggregate standardised test MSE by 11.05% relative to a parameter-matched Projector Control using the same irreducible projectors and complete linear equivariant space. The results support irreducible decomposition as an inductive bias for nonlinear higher-order equivariant processing.

title: Faster #PPM from faster #3SAT
author: László Kozma
abstract: The counting variant (#PPM) of the permutation pattern matching (PPM) problem asks for the number of occurrences of a permutation pattern in a host permutation of length $n$. The problem admits faster algorithms than the trivial $O^*(2^n)$ time enumeration; the best known running time, for both PPM and #PPM, is $O(1.415^n)$ (Gawrychowski and Rzepecki). It is also known that PPM is ETH-hard: an algorithm with running time $2^{o(n/\log{n})}$ would imply a subexponential algorithm for 3SAT (Jelínek, Opler, and Pekárek). We give a reduction in the opposite direction, showing that an algorithm for counting satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF formula (#3SAT) in time $2^{O({n}/{f(n)})}$, where $n$ is the number of variables, yields an algorithm for #PPM with running time $2^{O({n \sqrt{\log{f(n)}/{f(n)}}})}$. In particular, the recently claimed refutation of ETH by OpenAI implies a #3SAT algorithm with an improvement factor $f(n) \in Ω(\sqrt{\log{n}}/\log\log{n})$ in the exponent; this yields, through our reduction, a subexponential algorithm for #PPM.

title: Quantum amplification of improbable futures
author: Peter Maurice Catt
abstract: Some consequential futures consist of entirely plausible steps arranged into an unlikely sequence, such as ordinary weather anomalies combining into an extreme event or local equipment failures propagating into a widespread outage. Because the sequence as a whole carries little probability, it may be rarely observed in simulation. Quantum mechanics offers a way to change those odds: ideal amplitude amplification raises the chance of drawing such futures while preserving their relative likelihoods. For a five-state process six steps ahead, 13,888 of 15,625 futures are rare, yet together they account for about one draw in 40. We built the complete circuit in IBM's Qiskit and checked every part against an exact enumeration; four simulated rounds raised the share of rare futures drawn from 2.5% to 98.0%. On IBM's Kingston quantum computer, a two-step reference circuit that marks rare futures from a precomputed list drew them in 68.4% of shots against 43.5% for its control (z = 50); at three steps (about 1,170 two-qubit gates) the predicted signal reversed sign. Because this model's probabilities are known, every result could be checked against exact values; the mechanism is intended for simulators whose probabilities are hard to calculate, such as climate, epidemic and financial models.

title: Adaptive Dynamic Security for Operational Technology Against AI-Powered Attacks
author: Mohamed Chahine Ghanem
abstract: Operational technology now faces attackers whose tempo is set by AI. We present ADS-OT, an adaptive dynamic security framework modelling defensive posture as a partially observable decision problem. A reinforcement-learning policy adapts monitoring, access, deception, and segmentation under a safety-governance layer, reducing attack-path completion, detection, and containment versus static baselines.

title: When Can Unlabeled Data Pools Replace Membership Queries?
author: Dravyansh Sharma
abstract: Membership queries let a learner label arbitrary points and give near-optimal $\tilde O(n\log(1/\eps))$ label complexity for halfspaces under every marginal. A pool learner may label only sampled points. We ask when unlabeled data can replace membership queries. For homogeneous halfspaces the answer depends only on the angular law of $X/\|X\|$. If this law assigns zero mass to every hyperplane through the origin and positive mass to every nonempty open set of directions together with its reflection, a pool learner uses $O(n\log^3n\log(n/(\epsδ)))$ labels, uniformly over all such marginals and targets, without density, moment, concavity or isotropy assumptions. The same label bound holds for non-homogeneous halfspaces under every marginal with full support and no mass on affine hyperplanes, including Gaussians. Dropping either angular assumption admits $Ω(1/\eps)$ pool versus $O(\log(1/\eps))$ membership-query separations, even with unlimited unlabeled data. The price is paid in unlabeled data: in dimension $n\ge3$, for every unlabeled budget fixed in advance, some marginal satisfying both assumptions forces $Ω(1/\eps)$ labels. For isotropic $s$-concave marginals in dimension $n\ge3$, unlimited pools keep logarithmic label rates for every finite $s$. With an unlabeled budget fixed in advance, class-uniform polylogarithmic rates hold exactly for $s>-1/(n+1)$, or $s>-1/n$ under central symmetry, and in the general class the optimal rate between these thresholds is $\tildeΘ(\eps^{-(n-2)/n})$. This extends the range $s\ge-1/(2n+3)$ of previous sample-based guarantees, in the realizable setting.

title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics
author: Mingshan He
abstract: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.

title: Clifford synthesis is NP-complete
author: Søren Fuglede Jørgensen
abstract: We show that the problem of synthesizing a quantum circuit for a given Clifford operator using at most a specified amount of resources is NP-complete for several resource models of practical interest. Specifically, we study synthesis of a given Clifford operator using single-qubit Clifford gates and two-qubit Clifford gates, with full qubit connectivity and no additional ancilla qubits. With single-qubit gates free and CNOT as the only two-qubit gate, we show that deciding whether a given target admits an implementation using at most a specified number of CNOT gates is NP-complete, and we show that the problem remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is allowed and the budget counts all such gates. Moreover, we show that both results continue to hold when SWAP gates may be inserted for free, and when single-qubit gates are also considered part of the budget. In each case, we build on recent work by Li and Guan and show that there are polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to these decision problems, using a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices.

title: Predictive Maintenance at the Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained with Quantum Optimization
author: Filipe Chagas Ferraz
abstract: This article presents a predictive-maintenance pipeline that detects anomalies in bearings from vibration signals, adapted for deployment at the edge on low-cost microcontrollers, and that uses quantum optimization in two steps of its training. The pipeline consists of a step of vibration feature extraction and a step of classification with a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM). The features are selected by minimum redundancy and maximum relevance (mRMR) with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), under a limit on computing time. The OCSVM is adapted for inference at the edge without floating-point operations and is trained by a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE). In small-scale tests on a simulator, with the Paderborn bearing dataset, the VQE found the optimal selection in 36% of the runs with Adam, and PCE chose better support vectors than chance, until a classical local search made the two equal. A classical baseline, the usual OCSVM trained by SMO with its weights rounded, matched them without any search.

title: Learning Finite-Memory Binary Sources
author: Maciej Skorski
abstract: Estimating biased finite-memory sources from a single trajectory is a fundamental problem with practical impact, for example in estimating entropy for cryptography.
